lesson.title: Baud Rate: An Old Word for an Often-Misused Idea
lesson.summary: Baud rate is simply the historical name for symbol rate, named after telegraph engineer Emile Baudot, and the widespread habit of using it to mean bit rate is a genuine, common mix up worth clearing up.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter defined symbol rate as the number of distinguishable signal states a channel transmits per second. Baud rate is that exact same quantity under an older name; one baud simply means one symbol per second. The unit is named after Emile Baudot, a French telegraph engineer whose early digital code for transmitting text, an ancestor of later character encoding schemes, made his name a natural fit for a unit describing the rate of signal changes on a line. Historically, baud was the term that stuck in telegraphy and early modem engineering, while symbol rate is the more modern, modulation agnostic phrasing used across contemporary networking texts. Where one term appears, treat it as identical to the other.

The trouble is that baud rate and bit rate get used interchangeably in casual speech far more often than they should, and the previous chapter's whole point about symbol rate applies here with full force: baud rate only equals bit rate when each symbol carries exactly one bit. That was true of the earliest data communication equipment. The classic Bell 103 modem from the early days of dial up networking used simple binary frequency shift keying at 300 baud, and since each symbol carried exactly one bit, that modem is correctly described as both 300 baud and 300 bits per second, the numbers genuinely matching.

Later modem generations broke that equivalence on purpose. Telephone lines have a fairly narrow usable bandwidth, roughly the voice frequency range, which puts a hard physical ceiling on how many baud the line can reliably carry regardless of cleverness at either end. Modem designers who wanted higher throughput than that ceiling allowed could not simply raise the baud rate past what the line's bandwidth supported, so instead they raised the number of bits packed into each symbol, using denser modulation constellations such as QAM with many amplitude and phase combinations. A modem running at a modest baud rate could therefore report a bit rate many times higher than its baud rate, and popular usage never fully caught up: people kept saying baud when they meant bits per second, even on links where the two numbers had drifted far apart.

The habit is worth correcting because the distinction is not pedantic, it reflects a real physical limit. Baud rate is a statement about how fast a channel's physical signal is changing, constrained by the medium's bandwidth in a way you will see made precise in the channel capacity and Shannon theorem chapters just ahead. Bit rate is a statement about the throughput a user actually experiences, which depends on both the baud rate and the cleverness of the modulation scheme layered on top of it. Keeping the two words tied to the two different quantities they were built to describe makes the rest of the physical layer story, capacity limits, coding trade offs, and modulation choices, much easier to reason about correctly.
